title: Street Meat
synopsis: Hua hands Kyle the contract — extraction of an unnamed cargo from an Atlas-program continuation lab. The reason Kyle is the only freelancer who can complete the job is the same reason he ends up in the chair: the False Death Protocol his hardware carries is the only delivery method the facility's intake processes without flagging. Hua calls the Vultures. Kyle is delivered as a specimen, wakes on a slab, finds the cargo, recognizes who she is (Dr. Nadia Park, ex-NeoCortex Atlas neurointerface surgeon — the holy grail Kyle has been hunting since Seo died), and refuses to deliver her. He takes her to Pixel for a brief safe-pause; Sable arrives; Pixel begs him not to return to Hua. He goes anyway, because the code requires the contract be closed properly. Standard rate. Refunded. Then the chair.
html:
# Street Meat

*Protagonist: Kyle Ellen Corbin-Vasik*

## Act 1: The Contract

The south-arm chamber under the Cruciform Depot is the kind of room that has decided what it is and is not interested in being anything else. Concrete on three sides. Steel on the fourth. A single oak table at the center, two chairs, a bolted-to-the-floor steel chair against the far wall, and on the eastern side a heat rock under a low lamp where a juvenile saltwater crocodile sleeps. Sixty centimeters from snout to tail. The crocodile does not move when Kyle enters. Hua does not look up either. This is the first time Kyle has been in the chamber. He has been on the Lotus freelance roster six weeks — since Mira's interview on the West Town cross-street at oh-two-fourteen on the thirteenth of last month — and has not yet accepted a Lotus-tagged contract through Sable's pipeline. The Lotus side of the roster has accumulated three small unmet routings and zero in-person summons. Tonight Hua summoned him directly, bypassing Sable, which is its own kind of statement. Kyle is here because the summons did not pass through the channel he could refuse it through, and because the math of refusing a personal summons from a south-arm captain after six weeks of polite non-engagement is the math that made the summons necessary in the first place.

The NeoCortex catalogues the chamber in 0.3 seconds: four exits, three of them sealed, the fourth being the one he came in by. No augmented bodies in the room except his own. The crocodile registers in the array's biological-mass scan as an animal of approximately fourteen kilograms whose breathing pattern has not changed in the eleven seconds Kyle has been observing it. The lamp is a sodium-amber, fifteen watts, calibrated to keep the heat rock at thirty-two degrees Celsius. Kyle does not need any of this information. The hardware logs it anyway. The hardware logs everything.

Hua is fifty-something, compact, in a gray qipao that has been pressed that morning. Iron-grey hair cropped close at the sides. No augmentation, which the array confirms with the small absence-flag it produces for unaugmented bodies — the only person in the chamber whose hardware Kyle's array cannot map. She is reading a manila folder at the table. She has been reading it for the eleven seconds Kyle has been observing the crocodile. She finishes a page. Turns it. Finishes another.

*She read your file before the meeting. She is reading another file now. The meeting has not started yet because she has not decided it has.*

When the meeting starts, it starts because she closes the folder. Not because she stands. Not because she gestures. Because the folder is closed. Kyle reads the closing the way he would read a draw. The hardware does not speak.

"Sit, Corbin-Vasik. The chair is for the contract. You are not the contract yet."

He sits. The chair across from her is the one for visitors. The bolted chair against the far wall is the one she did not say *yet* about; she said *not yet*. The distinction is tactical. He files it.

She slides a single sheet across the table. The sheet has a manifest code, a payment figure (Φ47,000, half on accept, half on confirmation of delivery), a window (oh-three-hundred to oh-six-hundred, firm), and an address. The address is a corponation facility on the buffer-zone perimeter — Atlas-program continuation lab, Helix-subcontracted intake. He has run two extractions inside facilities of this taxonomy before. The taxonomy is on the page. The cargo is not.

He reads the sheet. He looks up.

"Cargo."

"A person. Researcher held under corporate constraint at the facility's research wing. Designated by the manifest code on the sheet. Cell 4-East, intake-zone-three. Ambulatory. Cooperative when the door opens — they have been told to expect an extraction tonight, they have not been told who. They will walk out of the cell under their own power once you are in the corridor with them."

"Name."

"Manifest code is the identifier I am giving you."

"Name."

Hua does not look up. "I am not naming the cargo. The cargo is the manifest code. Take the contract on the manifest code or do not take the contract."

*She is withholding the name. She has never withheld the name on a contract before. The withholding is information. Acting on it is also information.*

He does not act on it. The hardware runs the read on Hua's micro-expressions: the brow symmetry, the lip line, the small stillness around the eyes that belongs to people who have stopped performing. She is not lying about anything she has said. She is not telling him what she has not said. The two facts coexist the way they coexist with operators of her caliber — she has decided what to disclose and what to withhold, and the withholding is part of the contract design, and Kyle has known this about Hua's reputation since long before he ever sat across a table from her, because Hua's reputation is exactly the contract-designer reputation that produced the freelance roster offer at the cross-street six weeks ago. The withholding is the price of the roster being valuable. He has accepted that price in principle for six weeks.

Tonight the price has come due in person, and he is not certain the math holds. He files the uncertainty. He does not raise it.

"Why."

"Because if I tell you the name, your code refuses the contract before you walk out of this chamber, and the cargo dies in the research wing at oh-six-hundred. The cargo is alive at oh-six-hundred only if you take the contract on the code I am offering. I am not asking you to like the trade. I am offering you the trade. Take it or do not take it."

The hardware files this as the cleanest description Hua has ever given of how she works. Kyle hears it the way you hear a thesis. He does not let his face show the filing.

*She is telling you she knows your code. The telling is itself part of the contract design. She is buying your acceptance of the withholding by being honest about why she is withholding. The honesty is the trap. You see the trap. You are taking the contract anyway because the alternative is the cargo dying at oh-six-hundred, and the code does not have a clause that prefers a closed file at oh-six-hundred over a person walking out under your custody at oh-five-forty-five.*

The code does not have that clause. Kyle reads the rest of the sheet.

"Why me."

"You have completed three extractions from Helix-subcontracted Atlas-program continuation labs in the last twelve months. Two of them were facilities of the same security taxonomy as this one. Your reputation in this part of the work reaches farther than your roster file. The cargo will be in the cell at oh-three-twenty. The bay-three loading dock has its outbound window at oh-five-fifteen until oh-five-forty-five — that is your egress geometry, the rest of the bays roll on facility schedules I cannot adjust. The entry, the egress transport, and the routing to the rendezvous are your problem. I am not paying for the method. I am paying for the cargo at the rendezvous on the sheet at oh-six-hundred."

The hardware runs the math on what she has just said. The math is correct. Three extractions in twelve months, two of them at this taxonomy — Hua reads contracts the way she reads files, and the volume of Atlas-program-adjacent work he has been doing through Sable's pipeline lately is the kind of pattern that surfaces in any roster captain's quarterly review. She has not named the methods he used on the previous three. She does not need to. The pattern is the pattern. He is the freelancer she trusts to figure out an Atlas-program continuation lab's intake protocol because he has figured one out three times this year.

"Egress."

"Bay three rolls outbound at oh-five-fifteen until oh-five-forty-five, as I said — that is your geometry. After that the bay closes for the morning shift and the next scheduled outbound is at oh-eight-twenty, which is past your window for the cargo's window. You arrange whatever you arrange to receive the cargo at bay three before oh-five-forty-five. After that the contract is on the someone else and the someone else is going to be expensive."

Kyle does not respond. The hardware is already running the entry problem in parallel with the conversation. Helix-subcontracted Atlas-program continuation lab. The taxonomy is what he has run twice this year. Their perimeter is intake-grade, not active-pursuit-grade — the security model assumes nobody breaks *into* a place that processes the dead. The intake channel is calibrated for unaugmented donor bodies and Atlas-program specimens; the scanners flag tampering, not presence. An Atlas-program subject arriving as a corpse will be tagged as routine intake, processed through the cold-chain channel, and routed to a holding bay for autopsy queue. The holding bay is contiguous with the research wing. A walking subject from the holding bay to the research wing does not generate an alarm because the research wing's staff routinely move between the two. The exit through bay three is the standard outbound for processed material. The math resolves in 0.6 seconds.

*The False Death Protocol. The protocol is exactly what this facility's intake is calibrated to process without flagging. Atlas-program-subject corpse arriving via Vultures specimen-intake → holding bay slab → restart at the 240-second mark → walk to the cargo's cell through the research wing → exit through bay three with the cargo at the driver's window. The math is not complicated. The math is also costly. The protocol is the thing you do not advertise. The protocol is the thing you have used three times in your life, none of them recently, all of them in private. You are about to use it for a fourth.*

The hardware files the calculation. Kyle does not say *False Death Protocol* aloud. The protocol's existence is in his Atlas Division medical file and nowhere else, and the thing the protocol is most useful for is the thing it is most useful for *if no one knows you have it*. He has not advertised the protocol because the protocol's value is its invisibility. He is not going to advertise it now to a Lotus Syndicate captain who reads files for a living. He will arrange the Vultures pickup himself through his own contact at the federation's western dispatch node — a man named Dax who has driven two of his deliveries before, who does not ask questions, who will pick him up in an unmarked panel van at the alley behind the recycler substation Kyle has used as a rendezvous twice this year.

He says, neutral: "Acknowledged. The entry will be in place by oh-three-twenty."

Hua does not look up. "That is not a confirmation of method."

"You said you were not paying for the method."

"I am not. I am noting that you also did not specify it."

"That is correct."

Hua turns a page. "Thank you for not specifying it. The fewer people who know what you are about to do, the fewer people who can route the information past me by accident. I appreciate operators who do not advertise."

The hardware logs the sentence. The sentence is precise. The sentence does not say *I do not know what you are about to do*. The sentence says *the fewer people who know, the fewer who can route past me*. Hua may know. Hua may not know. The sentence is calibrated to be true either way. He files it. He does not act on it.

"Risks."

"Within parameters. The cargo will not resist extraction. The cargo has been told to expect you. The facility's security is intake-grade, not active-pursuit-grade. The exit window is the firm window. The driver is reliable."

*Reliable is what she calls things she has already paid for in advance. The cargo has been told to expect you. The cargo will be ready.*

He has the question in his head. He has had it since the moment Hua refused the name. The question is the question every operator in his line of work has to ask before accepting a withheld-cargo contract: *what kind of person is the cargo.* The kind of question that gets asked obliquely because the asking-directly costs something. Kyle has accepted withheld-cargo contracts twice in seven years. Both times the withholding was protective tradecraft — the contractor did not know the name in order to not be able to give it up under interrogation. Both times the cargo turned out to be exactly what Hua's framing implied. He is going to assume the same is true here because the assumption is the only assumption the contract permits him to make. He is also going to be wrong about it. The hardware does not yet know this. Neither does he.

He says: "Φ47,000 is below the rate for an extraction of a held researcher from an Atlas-program continuation lab. The standard would be sixty-five."

"The standard is sixty-five."

"Φ47 is a discount."

"Yes."

"Why."

Hua picks up the folder again. Opens it. Does not look up. "Because the contract is the contract. The price is the price. Take it or do not take it. The driver is at oh-two-hundred either way; if you do not take it I find someone else who can solve the entry, and the someone else will charge me the full sixty-five and run a forty percent failure probability, and I will pay it and absorb the failure, and the cargo will be a closed file by oh-six-hundred. The Φ18,000 discount is what you save me if I do not have to use the someone else."

The arithmetic is correct. The arithmetic is also designed. Kyle has not been in this room before, but he has been across desks and tables from operators of Hua's caliber for years, and he recognizes the shape of being told a true thing for a designed reason without needing prior in-person experience with this specific operator.

*She is telling you the truth because the truth is the trap. The trap is not the contract. The trap is the withholding. She bought your discipline by not telling you what you are discipline-ing toward.*

The hardware files this. Kyle does not act on it.

He takes the sheet. He folds it once. He puts it in the inside pocket of the jacket. He does not say *accepted*. The taking is the accepting. Hua has not looked up since she opened the folder the second time. The crocodile has not moved. The chamber is the chamber.

At the door, before he leaves, she says — without looking up — "Thank you for your time."

It is the first sentence she has said in eleven years that has felt to him like a conclusion.

---

## Act 2: The Vultures

The rendezvous is a service alley behind a recycler substation in the buffer zone. Kyle is there at oh-one-fifty-three. He has eaten — not at Mrs. Chen's, somewhere else, somewhere he can be unrecognized — a high-fat protein bar and two ounces of pure glucose paste, the kind of meal the False Death Protocol's restart curve responds to. The Cerebral Oxygenation Assist is at full reserve. The bio-battery is at sixty-two percent and climbing — as high as it will go without a hot meal he does not have time for. He has run the protocol three times in his life. None of them have been pleasant. The third was a controlled training event at Seo's insistence. Seo had stood beside the table the whole four minutes. Kyle is not running this one in front of anyone he trusts.

The Vultures truck arrives at oh-one-fifty-eight. Unmarked panel van, refrigerated, the Carrion Logistics LLC insignia in matte black on the left chest of the driver's gray uniform when he steps out — a tall man, mid-forties, no augmentation Kyle's array can detect, the bored efficiency of someone who has done this several times tonight already. He does not greet Kyle. He opens the back of the van. The interior is what Kyle expected: refrigerated cabin, four body-length compartments, two of them currently occupied with bodies the Vultures have been collecting on tonight's route. The driver gestures to the empty compartment second from the bay door. Kyle climbs in. The driver hands him a tag — a small adhesive strip with a barcode and a manifest number, the same manifest number from Hua's sheet. Kyle peels the backing and applies the tag to his own left wrist where the intake scanner will read it.

"Six minutes to the facility," the driver says. He does not look at Kyle. "You'll go through intake while you're under. Wake up on the slab in the holding bay. The slab will be at thirty-eight degrees. Don't sit up immediately — give the scanners ninety seconds to log you as ambient before you move. After that, you have approximately two and a half minutes before the next intake clerk's rotation. Bay three is the loading dock you want. The loading dock door is forty-six meters from the holding bay's southern exit."

Kyle looks at him. "You have done this before."

"Six times. The last one made it. The five before that did too. No one I have driven has yet failed to wake up. I do not know if the protocol fails sometimes; I only know that for me it has not."

"That is not statistically meaningful."

"No, it is not. But you should hear it before you stop your heart."

Kyle nods. The driver closes the back of the van. The interior is dark and cold. Kyle settles against the compartment wall, draws his knees up, places the tip of his right thumb at the precise interface point on his cardiac regulator at the left lateral throat, and runs the False Death Protocol's NeoCortex signal sequence.

The sequence is twenty-two characters long. He memorized it at sixteen. He has not used it in two years. The hardware recognizes it the way a lock recognizes a key.

*Three. Two.*

The regulator crashes into safe-mode flatline at the *one*. The Cerebral Oxygenation Assist activates at the *zero*. Kyle's heart stops. The 240-second timer begins. The world is not pain exactly. The world is the sound of his own pulse going away, and then the sound of his own pulse not being there to listen for, and then a quiet so specific it is not even quiet, it is just the absence of the frequency he has been listening to for twenty-seven years.

The last thing the hardware logs before the bio-battery routes to the assist is the truck's engine, cycling up, pulling away from the alley.

Then nothing.

---

He wakes on the slab.

The ceiling above him is low — institutional drop-tile, fluorescent panels, one panel flickering at a frequency the hardware logs as 47Hz, which is the frequency Helix-subcontracted facilities run their secondary lighting at. The slab is at thirty-eight degrees as the driver said it would be. Kyle does not move. The hardware runs the diagnostic: bio-battery at fifty-one percent (the protocol cost ten and a half), cardiac regulator restarted on the documented schedule, Cerebral Oxygenation Assist returning to standby with three minutes thirty seconds of reserve unused, all sensor channels nominal. He counts to ninety. He does not move. The 47Hz panel flickers above him. Somewhere out of his sightline, an intake scanner cycles a soft chime — his ambient logging, the body's heat signature finally registering as living-and-not-anomalous. The chime resolves into the silence of a room a building has decided is empty. He sits up.

The holding bay is small — four slabs in the row he is on, two in another row at right angles, all of them empty except his own. The walls are the same drop-tile as the ceiling. The lighting is low and clinical. There is one door at the southern wall, closed, and the door has the thin red diode that means it is sealed pending intake-clerk authorization. He has approximately two and a half minutes before the rotation. The bay is empty of people. The cargo is not here. The cargo is in Cell 4-East, intake-zone-three, which the facility's standard schematic places approximately eighty meters east through the maintenance corridor and into the research wing.

Kyle works the lock-override on the southern door with the pry bar and the wire from the small bag he tied at his belt before the protocol. The kit the Vultures' driver did not inspect because Vultures drivers do not inspect anything. The lock cycles in nine seconds. The diode goes from red to green. He pulls the small adhesive tag off his left wrist and crushes the barcode under his thumb until the strip cracks. The tag is now unreadable. The intake log will mark him as either a tampered-tag specimen or as departed-without-clearance. Either way, the next intake clerk's rotation is going to find a problem. He has between two and three minutes before that becomes his problem too.

He opens the door. The maintenance corridor is empty.

---

The corridor is the standard Helix-subcontracted secondary-site geometry — narrow, low ceilings, the institutional gray of a building that has decided color is a maintenance cost it would rather not pay. The hardware overlays the schematic the array harvested from the badge-reader frequency three hours ago against the actual geometry as Kyle moves. The two match within tolerances. He is forty-six meters from the eastern junction where the corridor branches into the research wing. The research wing is where Cell 4-East is. The research wing is also where the on-shift staff are — a low-density night cycle, four people across two floors per Helix's standard staffing model, three of them in the lab on the upper floor, one of them on patrol rotation at the lower-floor desk. The lower-floor desk is between Kyle and Cell 4-East.

He moves. He moves the way he has moved through corridors at this taxonomy three times this year — efficient, low, the array tracking the patrol officer's electromagnetic signature through the wall before Kyle is in the wall's adjacent corridor. The signature is at the desk. The signature is stationary. The signature has been stationary for at least the duration of Kyle's last forty meters of approach, which means the officer is reading something or eating something or sleeping something off, and any of those answers to the geometry question is acceptable.

The desk comes around a corner. The officer is reading. He does not see Kyle until Kyle is two meters from the desk. The hardware reads the draw the moment the officer's hand twitches toward the holster — Ballistic Precognition firing passive, the read arriving at Kyle's body 0.4 seconds before the officer's hand finishes the motion — and Kyle's body is already moving, already past the line where the round will be, already at the officer's side with the joint-lock at the wrist and the pressure release at the brachial plexus. The officer folds. Kyle catches him before the body hits the floor (the catching is acoustic, not kindness — a body hitting institutional flooring is louder than the discipline can afford), zip-ties the wrists to the leg of the desk, and is past the desk and into the research wing's main corridor in under nine seconds.

Cell 4-East is at the end of the row. The corridor is empty. The cells along the corridor are mostly dark — the wing operates on a research staff's day-shift cycle, most of its occupants sedated or sleeping at this hour. Cell 4-East has a low light burning behind the viewport. The light is not the cell's overhead. The light is something the cell's occupant has on at oh-three-twenty in the morning because the cell's occupant is awake and is reading something.

Kyle works the cell's lock with the pry bar and the wire. Nine seconds.

The door opens.

She is forty-three. Compact. Korean — monocultural Korean, the array confirms before Kyle's conscious thought finishes the sentence, ninety-nine percent ancestry by the array's phenotype-read at the resolution it can run at fifty-one percent bio-battery, the rare and statistically improbable kind of monoculture that registers in the GLMZ as anomaly before it registers as person. Black hair short, threaded with the first iron-grey at the temples. Glasses with thin metal frames. Plain dark cotton long-sleeve top. Surgical-grade hands holding a small leather case in her lap. She is sitting on the bunk reading a printed journal under a lamp she has clipped to the bunk's frame because the cell's overhead is on the night-low setting. She looks up.

*Phenotype confirmed before person was named. The catalogue order is information. You do not have time to examine which kind.*

She closes the journal. She sets it on the bunk. She picks up the leather case and stands. The motion is unhurried. She has been told to expect an extraction tonight — Hua said so on the sheet, *the cargo has been told to expect you* — and she is responding to the door opening the way you respond to a thing you have been told would happen. She does not look surprised. She does not look afraid. She looks at Kyle the way she would look at a colleague she does not yet know but has been told to cooperate with.

"You are early," she says. American-academic English with the precise geometry of a non-native speaker who learned the language as the medium of her profession. "They told me oh-three-thirty."

"We are leaving," Kyle says. He has not yet given his name. He is not going to. Hua's manifest code is on the cell's external tag and Kyle has matched it against the sheet and the matching is the only credential the contract requires. "Now."

"Yes," she says. She tucks the leather case under her left arm. She steps out of the cell. She closes the door behind her — a small, precise motion, the door pulled to the latch but not locked, the kind of leaving-tidy that someone does when they do not want the people coming to look for them in the morning to immediately know which way they went. The hardware files this. He does not comment.

They start back down the corridor at a measured walk. She matches his pace within two steps. The eastern junction is forty meters ahead. The bay-three loading dock is sixty meters past the junction.

They make it twenty meters before the second patrol officer comes around the eastern junction's far corner.

This one has been on the second-floor lab and is descending — the array reads the descent because the second-floor staircase exits into the same junction the cell corridor opens onto, and the descending body has the specific motor signature of someone who knows the building and is moving with intent toward the lower-floor desk where the first officer was supposed to be. He sees Kyle first. He sees the cell tag on the wall behind Kyle's shoulder second. He sees the doctor third. The hardware times the reads: 0.2 seconds, 0.3 seconds, 0.4 seconds. Total recognition window: 0.9 seconds.

The officer's right hand moves toward the holster. Augmented, this one — chrome-laced reflex augment at the right temple, the array catalogues it, the augment's motor-bus spike is measurable as a clean electromagnetic bloom 0.3 seconds before the hand finishes its motion. Ballistic Precognition fires passive. The read arrives at Kyle's body before the officer's body knows what its body is about to do.

Kyle steps left and forward — not back, into the angle the round will not occupy — and the officer fires, and the shot goes through the space Kyle's chest was occupying 0.3 seconds ago, and the round hits the wall behind him, and Kyle is already inside the officer's reach with the pry bar against the chrome bracket at the temple. One precise contact. The reflex augment shorts. The officer's draw arm goes loose, the second shot does not come, and Kyle puts him on the floor with a knee to the back of the leg and zip-ties the wrists to the corner brace of the junction wall.

Eleven seconds. Both officers down. Forty meters to bay three.

He turns to the doctor.

She is two meters back, where she stopped when the first round fired. The leather case is still under her left arm. Her right hand is at her mouth — not in the gesture of someone who is about to scream, in the gesture of someone who has just witnessed a thing she has read about in journals. The pupils are dilated. The breath is the small involuntary intake at the back of the throat. She is not looking at the officer on the floor. She is looking at Kyle.

She lowers the hand. The voice is small, controlled, the cadence of a person composing the sentence in real time as the sentence forms.

*"Ballistic Precognition... Incredible."* she gasped.

The word she uses is the program's internal designation. She does not use the marketing name. She does not use the consumer-grade colloquialism. She uses the term Atlas Division put on the intake forms and the discharge summaries and the trial-protocol documents that Kyle has not seen since he was seventeen. The capability she just named was the one she filed under *theoretical at this density* because the only people she had ever seen run it were dead. She is not naming the capability. She is *recognizing* it. The recognition comes from a specific place. The specific place has a specific name.

The hardware files her. The filing is instant. The cognitive baseline implant at her left mastoid (Atlas Division employment badge, dormant, unrevoked) which the array had registered when the cell door opened and which Kyle had not yet examined because there had not been time to examine it. The surgical-grade dexterity profile. The way she had stood from the bunk — settled into the geometry of someone who has spent twenty years bent over operating tables. The leather case — the calibration toolchain, Kyle recognizes it now from the photographs Atlas Division never let leak. The age. The monocultural Korean phenotype. The English that learned itself as the medium of her profession.

She is the doctor. She is ex-NeoCortex Atlas Division. She walked off the program and has been salaried-silent for two years and the silence was about to end because Hua hired Kyle to deliver her to Hua, and Hua did not name her because Hua had read his file and Hua knew that if she had named the cargo as an Atlas Division surgeon, Kyle's code would have refused the contract before he walked out of Hua's chamber.

Kyle does not move. The officer at his feet is unconscious. The corridor behind the doctor is empty. The corridor ahead of them is empty. They have approximately four minutes before the upper-floor lab notices the missing patrol officer and routes a check.

The arithmetic resolves in 0.4 seconds.

*The contract requires you to deliver this woman to Hua of the Lotus Syndicate. The code requires you not to deliver her to Hua of the Lotus Syndicate. The code wins. The code always wins. The contract is now a contract you will complete only the extraction half of. The delivery is going to be to Sable, off-GLMZ, by oh-eight-hundred. You will refund Hua's half-payment afterward and walk back into her chamber to close the contract from your side, because the code requires the closing. You will go in the chair for the closing. The chair is the cost. The cost is named. The cost is acceptable.*

The arithmetic is complete in 0.4 seconds. Kyle does not let his face show the arithmetic. The doctor is still looking at him.

"Doctor," he says. The first word he has said to her with the title acknowledged. "We are leaving. Now."

She nods. The dilated pupils stabilize. The hand goes back to the leather case. The discipline she has been keeping for ten years engages and she becomes immediately competent again.

"Bay three," she says. "Sixty meters. Permitted route through the maintenance corridor. I have walked it twice."

"Walked."

"They permit me certain perimeter freedoms within the wing. I have been logged as cooperative."

"Then you are going to walk it a third time."

They go.

---

The maintenance corridor is sixty meters as the doctor said. They walk it in just under a minute. The bay-three loading dock door is unsealed at this hour because the bay is in active use — a Vultures truck Kyle does not recognize is in bay one offloading, two delivery clerks are in bay two with a refrigerated pallet, and bay three is empty except for the small panel van Kyle's contact at the federation's western dispatch node has parked there. Dax. The same tall man, mid-forties, unaugmented, who picked Kyle up at the recycler-substation alley three hours ago and delivered Kyle's flatlined body to the facility's specimen-intake channel and has now circled back per the second half of the schedule Kyle filed at oh-one-forty-five — a federation egress, federation rate, no Lotus routing in the paperwork. Dax leans against the van with a hand-rolled smoke and the same bored efficiency he had at the alley. Dax has driven two of Kyle's deliveries before. Dax does not ask questions.

Kyle walks Doctor Park toward the van. Dax sees them. Dax registers Doctor Park — that the cargo is ambulatory, walking out under her own power, with a leather case and a freelancer at her elbow. Dax registers, in the way Vultures drivers register everything, that this is a different shape of cargo than the contract sheet specified at the western-dispatch desk three hours ago. Dax puts the smoke out under his boot.

"Change of route," Kyle says. He does not slow down. He has Doctor Park by the elbow now, gentle, the doctor walking at his pace because she has decided to. "Drop us at the West Town safehouse instead of the rendezvous. Federation rate, plus the difference."

Dax looks at him for a count of four. The hardware times it. Dax does the math the same way a Vulture driver does the math: the federation contract Kyle filed at oh-one-forty-five specified an egress destination Kyle now wants changed; the change costs Dax nothing the original schedule was paying him because the original schedule was Kyle's federation contract end-to-end; the change gains him the difference Kyle is offering against the West Town safehouse routing; the math is *which rate Kyle is paying on the way back, and whether the cargo fits the original specification*. The cargo is ambulatory rather than refrigerated. The federation has standing language for ambulatory cargo. The standing language is more expensive than refrigerated. Kyle is offering federation rate plus the difference. Dax is a federation driver. The math is not neutral.

Dax opens the back of the van.

"West Town safehouse," he says. "Forty-three minutes. I will not stop for anything."

Kyle helps Doctor Park into the back. The doctor does not say anything. The doctor takes the bench seat near the cab, sets the leather case on her lap, and folds her hands over it. Kyle sits across from her. Dax closes the back. The van pulls out. The bay-three loading dock fades behind them. The hardware runs the timeline: oh-three-thirty-two when they leave the dock, oh-four-fifteen at the West Town safehouse, oh-four-thirty if Sable can route a pickup. Kyle opens the encrypted relay.

Sable answers in two seconds.

"Kyle."

"I have her. The cargo is the doctor — Park, ex-Atlas, the one I have been looking for. I am bringing her to the West Town safehouse. I need you there in thirty minutes. She is going off-GLMZ tonight."

The pause is one second. Sable does not waste pauses. "Off-GLMZ where."

"Wherever you can put her that no one in Lotus can reach."

Another second. Kyle hears the small mechanical sound of her ocular implants adjusting — she is reading the data feed in real time, recalculating the routes, the safehouses, the pickups, the favors, the whole map.

"I can put her on the Pulse at oh-five-twenty out of Lakeshore Terminal. Rotterdam in forty-three minutes. From Rotterdam I can route her into a free-floating sector by oh-eight-hundred. Total cost to my network: significant. Total cost to you: a favor I will name later."

"Take it."

"Done. I will be at the West Town safehouse in twenty-eight minutes."

The relay closes. Kyle looks at Doctor Park. Doctor Park is looking at him with the precise expression she had when she lowered her hand from the corridor wall — the researcher waiting for a result. He does not say anything. There is nothing to say yet. The van turns onto the buffer-zone arterial. The hardware cycles down to the diagnostic baseline. The bio-battery climbs.

*You did not deliver. The code held. The contract is broken. The contract being broken is the contract Hua designed for. She wins on every fork. You are picking which of her wins she gets, and the one you are picking is the one with the chair.*

Kyle knows this. He has known this since the moment the doctor named the read in the corridor. He keeps not saying anything. The doctor cleans her glasses on the hem of her shirt. The van runs.

## Act 3: The Pivot

The West Town safehouse is the side door at The Pivot — Kyle's building, his floor, his unit. He has not had the doctor anywhere else. The driver drops them at the alley entrance at oh-four-eleven, drives away without looking back, and Kyle takes Doctor Park up the back stairs and unlocks 2F and lets her in. He sets the chain on the door behind them.

The doctor stands in the middle of the room. She does not sit down. She catalogues the unit the way Kyle would catalogue a room: medkit by the door, notebook on the counter, the photograph of his mother on the windowsill facing the intersection because she would have wanted to see the street, the friction sheath for the katana on the hook beside the kitchen archway, the specific spareness of a person who lives alone and has made decisions about what he will keep. She looks at the photograph for slightly longer than the rest. She does not comment.

Kyle goes across the hall to 2E and knocks.

Pixel opens it on the third knock. She is in the oversized sweater and the steel-toed boots even at oh-four-fifteen — the boots on means she has been working, the sweater means it is cold in the unit, the absence of music means she is concentrating. She takes one look at Kyle and says, level, the way she always says it: "What is in the apartment."

"A doctor. Ex-NeoCortex Atlas Division. I need her safe for fifteen minutes until Sable picks her up."

"Why is she here and not in your safehouse."

"This is my safehouse."

"Kyle. This is your *home*."

"Yes."

Pixel looks at him for one full second. She does not perform the look — it is the calibration look, the one she uses when she is checking whether his hardware is the thing producing the decision. She decides it is not. She picks up the small toolkit she keeps by the door and she walks across the hall ahead of him.

In 2F, Doctor Park is at the kitchen counter, the leather case on the counter beside her, looking out the small kitchen window at the street. Pixel comes in. Pixel looks at the doctor. The doctor looks at Pixel.

*The phenotype read on Pixel registers Northern European 57 / Eastern European 28 / Southern European 15 — a face the GLMZ would describe as legibly pale. The phenotype read on the doctor registers Korean 99 — a face the GLMZ has not seen in years. The doctor has just been read in 0.4 seconds. The doctor knows she has been read. The reading is mutual.*

"Hi," Pixel says. The brightness is not real. The brightness is a calibrated weapon. "I am Pixel. I live across the hall. I am Kyle's neighbor and the person who maintains his hardware and the person who calibrated the lateral-array thermal-stress markers two weeks ago that he has not addressed yet."

The doctor cleans her glasses on the hem of her shirt. She puts the glasses back on. She nods. "Park Na-Young," she says. "Nadia. I am the person Kyle was contracted to deliver to a Lotus Syndicate captain tonight. He decided not to. He is now a person who has decided not to deliver me to a Lotus Syndicate captain, which is the kind of decision that has consequences I do not yet know the full shape of. I am told I will be picked up shortly."

"Yes," Pixel says, and the brightness is now openly hostile, "by Sable, who is a fixer who routes contracts and who I have known longer than you have. I suppose you are going to tell me you can do something about the lateral-array thermal-stress markers I have not yet addressed because I am, what was it, a girl with a soldering iron and you are a credentialed neurosurgeon."

The doctor looks at Pixel. The doctor does not perform the look. She looks the way she would look at an electrode array she is reviewing for calibration. Her glasses do not need cleaning again. She cleans them anyway.

"I would not phrase it that way," the doctor says. "You have done good work with bad documentation. The lateral-array drift you flagged two weeks ago is a firmware issue, not a hardware issue. Whoever calibrated him last did the right thing with the wrong tool. The correction is documented in a manual the program never released and that I happen to have memorized. If Kyle ever needs the manual, I can write it out. The work you have done since the last calibration has been creative. *Creative* is the word the program used for what someone does when they do not have access to the documentation but produce the right outcome anyway. It is a compliment. I do not know how to phrase it so that it does not sound condescending. I am sorry for that. I have spent a lot of years in rooms where the only register I had was the technical one."

Pixel stares at her.

Then Pixel turns to Kyle.

"She is being *gracious* at me," Pixel says, and the word *gracious* is an indictment, "and I cannot find anywhere to land the response. She is too good at this. I am going to need three days to figure out how to be properly angry about this and I do not have three days. Kyle, why is this happening in my building."

"Because the building is also my building," Kyle says, and he means it as a deflection, but it lands as a fact, and Pixel registers the fact, and the doctor registers Pixel registering the fact, and the room re-balances itself in the small way rooms re-balance when three people who have not previously been in the same room at the same time decide who is in charge of which silence.

The doctor sets her leather case on Kyle's small kitchen table. "While we are waiting," she says, "would you like me to look at the lateral array."

Kyle says: "No."

The doctor nods. "That is the correct answer at this time. There is a long answer about why you would benefit from saying yes eventually, and a different long answer about why you should not say yes tonight, and we do not have time for either. I am not going to press. I am going to put the case back in my hand." She picks the case up. She returns to the counter. She does not look at Pixel again, but she does say, in the same level voice: "I would have done good work with what you have. I am glad he has had it. I am leaving in approximately eleven minutes. The arrangement is not permanent. The work you have been doing is keeping him alive. I would like that to continue."

Pixel does not respond. Pixel cannot respond, because the only response available is gratitude or rage and she will not perform either in front of the doctor, and the doctor knows this, and the doctor is using the knowing the way a researcher uses a known variable. Kyle sees Pixel decide to file the encounter for later examination and to exit the room while she still can.

Pixel exits the room. She closes the door behind her.

In the hallway outside 2F, Pixel says — quietly, the way she says things when she does not want them to count as said — "I hate her so much."

Kyle, on the inside of the door, hears her. He does not respond. The doctor is at the counter cleaning her glasses again. The doctor heard too. The doctor is pretending she did not.

*Pixel is not wrong. Pixel is also not right. The doctor is what the doctor is, and the doctor has not done anything wrong. Pixel knows this. The hatred is the kind that forms when the world produces a person who is what you would be if your life had gone differently and they happen to be in your building at four in the morning. File it. Do not act on it. There is not time.*

There is not time. Sable arrives at oh-four-twenty-eight, which is six minutes earlier than her stated estimate, which is the kind of margin Sable arranges when the math is tight. She comes up the back stairs in the tan coat with her hands in the pockets and her ocular implants adjusting to the unit's lighting and her face composed in the precise stillness of a fixer who has decided that the next fifteen minutes are the most expensive fifteen minutes of her quarter. She does not knock; Kyle has the door open before she reaches it. She steps inside. She looks at the doctor.

"Doctor Park," she says.

"Sable," the doctor says. "I have been told to expect you."

"You have been told correctly. We have nineteen minutes to be at Lakeshore Terminal. Pulse 0520 to Rotterdam. From Rotterdam I have a route to a destination I will not name in this room. The destination is reasonable. You will not be comfortable. You will be unfindable."

The doctor nods. She picks up the leather case. She looks at Kyle.

"Thank you," she says.

Kyle does not say *you are welcome*. He does not have a category for what to say. The hardware does not produce a recommendation. He nods. He does not look away from her. She cleans her glasses one more time on the hem of her shirt and she follows Sable to the door.

At the door, Sable stops. She looks back at Kyle. She does not perform the look — she just looks, the implants logging him at the resolution she runs at when she has decided to remember a thing.

"Hua is going to know within the hour," Sable says.

"I know."

"You are going back."

"Yes."

"Why."

Kyle thinks about the answer for a half-second. The hardware does not have an answer. The code has the answer. The code does not articulate well in language. He says:

"Because the contract is the contract. Hua paid me at half. I am going to give her her money back. The contract is going to close from my side because that is the only side it can close from now."

Sable looks at him. The implants make their small adjustment. She does not say *do not go*. She has known him long enough to know that *do not go* is not a sentence he hears.

She says: "I will take care of her."

"I know."

The door closes behind them. The unit is quiet. The doctor's leather case is gone. The kitchen is the kitchen. The photograph of his mother is on the windowsill facing the intersection. Kyle stands in the middle of the room. The hardware diagnostic resumes its baseline cycle.

*Pixel.*

Kyle goes across the hall and knocks on 2E.

Pixel opens it on the first knock. She has been standing at the door. She has heard Sable arrive and Sable leave. She knows what is coming because she has known what is coming since the moment Kyle said *this is my safehouse*.

"Don't go," Pixel says.

"I have to."

"You don't."

"I do."

"Kyle. Hua does not require you to bring the money back. The contract was paid at half. If you do not bring the money back, she calls in the half she paid as a debt and it accrues, and you owe her, and that is bad. If you do bring the money back, you are walking into her chamber having just refused her contract, and she puts you in the chair. The chair, Kyle. The actual chair. The one that is bolted to the floor. The one that — " Pixel stops herself. The breath is shaking in the way her breath shakes when she is trying not to perform the shaking. "I have looked at the casualty patterns from every freelancer who has refused a Lotus contract in the last four years. The pattern is the chair. The pattern is hands. The pattern is — "

"Pixel."

" — Kyle. The pattern is *hands*."

"Pixel. I know."

She looks at him. Her face does the thing it does when she is processing — the small flicker of the eyes as the catalogue runs — and then she looks at his hands. He still has them. They are at his sides. The hardware logs Pixel looking at them. He does not move them.

"You know," she says.

"Yes."

"And you are going."

"Yes."

"Why."

"Because the code is the code. Because if I do not close the contract from my side, Hua holds the half-payment as a debt, and the debt sits as ambient leverage that ages without spending, and I will spend the next two years not knowing when she calls it. If I close the contract — refund the money, walk in, walk out — the debt is settled at the cost of whatever she chooses to do to me when I walk in. The cost will be high. It will not be infinite. The debt would be infinite. I am picking the lower cost."

Pixel closes her eyes. "You are picking the cost that takes your hands."

"I am picking the cost I can name."

"Kyle."

"Pixel. I know."

She opens her eyes. She looks at him. She does not cry. She has not cried in front of him in three years and she is not going to start now, because the not-crying is part of the convention they have built, and the convention is the only thing keeping either of them upright at this hour. She nods. The nod is small. The nod is acceptance. The nod is the most expensive nod Pixel has ever given him.

"Come back," she says.

"I will try."

"Try harder than that."

"I will."

She steps back. She closes the door. He hears the lock cycle. He hears her take three steps away from the door inside the unit and stop. He stands in the hall for two seconds. Then he goes back to 2F. He picks up Silence from the hook by the kitchen archway. He settles the friction sheath across his back. He picks up the credit chip from the kitchen drawer — the half-payment Hua gave him three hours ago, untouched, the chip still in the evidence sleeve the syndicate banker put it in. He puts the chip in the inside pocket of the jacket where Hua's manifest sheet lives.

He leaves 2F. He locks the door. He goes down the back stairs.

The rain is still going. Outside the alley, the GLMZ is in the small hours where the city pretends to sleep. Kyle walks south toward the Cruciform Depot. He does not call Sable. He does not call Pixel. He does not call anyone. The chip is in his pocket. The blade is on his back. The code is the code.

## Act 4: The Refund

The south-arm chamber is exactly as it was at oh-one-twenty when he sat down across from Hua and took the contract. The crocodile is on the heat rock. The lamp is at fifteen watts. The folding chair is bolted to the floor against the far wall. Hua is at the table reading a different folder this time. She closes it when Kyle steps through the door. She does not say *sit*.

There are two of her men against the eastern wall now. There were not at oh-one-twenty. Both of them have augmented forearms and the small twitch at the right temple that marks reflex augments at full draw. The senior lieutenant — the one who has been with her twenty years, the one she asks about his mother every Tuesday — is at the door behind Kyle, between Kyle and the only exit. Kyle's array catalogues all three before his foot has finished the third step into the room.

Kyle takes the chip out of his pocket. He walks to the table. He sets the chip on the table in front of Hua. He stays standing.

"Standard rate," he says. The voice is the voice he has practiced for a long time. "Refunded."

Hua looks at the chip. She does not pick it up.

The arithmetic resolves in his interior, in the silence the chamber has trained itself to hold. The hardware is not the thing that is doing the arithmetic. The code is doing the arithmetic. The code says:

*She picked you because your reputation at extractions of this taxonomy was the only freelance reputation on the roster that meant the entry would solve itself. She did not specify the method. She did not need to. She trusted you to find one. The method you found is your secret. The fact that you found one was hers to count on. That was the capability variable — not the specific hardware she could not have read off your file, but the demonstrated track record, which is the variable any contract designer reads off a roster. That was the reason your name was on the sheet before she opened the folder.*

*She withheld the cargo's identity because she had read your file. She knew that if the cargo was named, your code would refuse the contract before the door opened. The facility intake would not happen. The doctor would stay where she was. The worst outcome for Hua. So she withheld. The withholding got you through the door. After the door, your choice was the variable.*

*She designed the contract knowing all three forks served her. Deliver, and the syndicate has the doctor. Refuse, and the doctor is still extracted from the enemy facility, just into someone else's hands; the original threat is still neutralized, and Hua now has cause to take an unaffiliated freelancer's hands and demonstrate Lotus's reach. Die in the extraction, and the doctor is disrupted, the contract written off, the message sent. Every fork served her.*

*You are now executing a fork she did not model. Refuse, return the money, close the contract from your side. The contract closes properly at her cost. She does not retain the half-payment as ambient debt. She does not get the doctor. She has nothing she can account for except the chair. The chair is no longer the second product on her invoice. The chair is the only product. And the chair as the only product, after a contract she designed to have multiple products, is a smaller win than she budgeted for.*

*She is going to take the chair anyway. The chair is what is now available to her. Refusing the chair would be admitting the contract failed at her end. She will not admit that. The chair will happen.*

*The chair is the cost. The cost is named. The cost is acceptable.*

The arithmetic is complete in 0.6 seconds.

Hua looks up from the chip. She looks at Kyle. She does not smile. She does not frown. She does the thing she does, which is read his face the way she reads files. The reading takes four seconds. The hardware times it.

"You returned the money," Hua says.

"Yes."

"That was not on the form."

"No."

She is quiet for another two seconds. The crocodile breathes. The lamp hums at the frequency the lamp always hums at. The two men at the eastern wall do not move. The senior lieutenant at the door behind Kyle does not move either.

Then Hua says, level, the way she has said *Thank you for your time* at the end of every meeting Kyle has had with her in this chamber:

"I am going to need to think about that."

She nods at the senior lieutenant.

The senior lieutenant moves. He is fast — twenty years of being the senior lieutenant in this chamber has made him fast — and Kyle's array reads the motor-bus spike at the lieutenant's forearm 0.3 seconds before the strike comes, and the array routes the read clean, and Kyle's body knows which way to step, and the body does not step.

The body does not step because the body has accepted the cost. The code has accepted the cost. The chair is the cost. The chair is named. Stepping out of the strike would mean Kyle was now in a room with three armed men and the senior lieutenant and the only exit blocked, and he would have to fight his way out, and the fighting would mean he had not actually refunded the contract — he had refunded the chip and then refused the consequence, which is not a refund, which is not the closure of the contract from his side, which is just paperwork.

The code is not paperwork.

Kyle does not step.

The shock-baton hits the chrome bracket in his jaw at exactly the angle the lieutenant has practiced for twenty years to hit it. The pain is a specific frequency, sharp and then radiating, and the hardware logs *IMPACT — LEFT MANDIBLE — CHROME BRACKET CONTACT — SEVERITY: SIGNIFICANT*, and the floor comes up. The floor is concrete. The floor smells of water that has been in the chamber a long time. Kyle's left shoulder hits the floor first, then the side of his head, then the rest of him. The hardware does not lose consciousness — the bio-battery is at fifty-eight percent and the impact was below the threshold for cardiac shock — but the body is on the floor, and the men are coming around the table, and the chair against the far wall is the chair that has been the chair since before Kyle was born.

Hua is still seated at the table. She has not stood. She is not going to stand. She watches the lieutenant and the two men lift Kyle off the floor and carry him to the chair. She watches them strap his wrists to the bolted arms of the chair with the specific cargo strap the chamber keeps in the drawer of the table for exactly this purpose. She watches them check that the straps are at the correct tension. Then she stands up, walks to the small refrigerated cabinet on the eastern wall — the one she keeps the crocodile's food in — and opens it with the key she keeps on her person. She takes out a wrapped bundle. She closes the cabinet. She walks back to the table.

She sets the bundle on the table next to Kyle's chip.

She unwraps it. The bundle is a cleaver — heavy, single-edged, the kind of cleaver a butcher uses on a side of pork — with a cauterizer band wrapped around the back of the blade. The cauterizer band is the EMT-spec preservation model. The kind that seals the wound at the same moment it makes the cut. The kind that keeps the severed thing alive long enough for someone to take it to an AutoDoc.

Kyle is in the chair. He is awake. The hardware is awake. The chrome bracket in his jaw is sending a steady ache up the left side of his face. The straps are at the correct tension. The lieutenant is at his right. The two men are at his left.

Hua looks at the cleaver. She looks at Kyle. Her face does not change.

"I am going to do this myself," she says. "I owe you that much."

Kyle does not respond. There is no response that the convention will accept.

The crocodile breathes on the heat rock. The lamp hums. The chamber holds.

Hua picks up the cleaver.
